checkpoints.question: Why is it better to integrate security activities into every phase of the SSDLC rather than adding security after development is complete?

options.A: Building security into each phase of development is more cost-effective and less disruptive than adding it after completion
options.B: Security requirements can only be defined during the requirements phase of the SSDLC
options.C: Integrating security at every phase means developers do not need to write code reviews
options.D: Adding security early prevents developers from writing any code that could contain vulnerabilities

checkpoints.explanation: The section explicitly states that retrofitting security into finished software is more expensive, less effective, and more disruptive than building it in from the start, making early integration the preferred approach.

checkpoints.question: What is the key difference between allowlist validation and denylist validation?

options.A: Allowlist validation works on client-side systems while denylist validation works server-side
options.B: Allowlist validation accepts only known-good input and rejects everything else
options.C: Allowlist validation uses regular expressions while denylist validation uses type checking
options.D: Denylist validation rejects known-bad patterns and accepts everything else by default

checkpoints.explanation: The section defines allowlist as accepting only known-good input and denylist as accepting everything except known-bad patterns, and explicitly states allowlist is the most secure approach.

checkpoints.question: Why must server-side validation always run, even if client-side validation is also present?

options.A: Server-side validation is required because browsers do not understand client-side code
options.B: Server-side validation is the only method that enforces data type constraints
options.C: Client-side validation causes performance problems that server-side validation solves
options.D: Client-side validation can be bypassed by disabling JavaScript or using a web proxy

checkpoints.explanation: The section explicitly states that client-side validation is trivially bypassed by disabling JavaScript, modifying requests with a web proxy, or sending raw HTTP requests, so the server must never trust it has already happened.

checkpoints.question: What is the purpose of output encoding?

options.A: Output encoding validates that user input matches an expected format before display
options.B: Output encoding prevents attackers from accessing the application source code
options.C: Output encoding converts user data into a safe form so it is treated as data, not code
options.D: Output encoding compresses user data to reduce the size of HTTP responses

checkpoints.explanation: The section defines output encoding as converting user-supplied data into a safe representation before it appears in application output, so the browser treats it as data, not code.

checkpoints.question: Which encoding method separates SQL code structure from user-supplied values at the database driver level?

options.A: URL encoding converts special characters to percent format for safe transmission
options.B: HTML encoding converts special characters to entity equivalents for safe display
options.C: JavaScript encoding prevents scripts from executing in the browser context
options.D: Parameterized queries and prepared statements separate SQL code structure from user-supplied values

checkpoints.explanation: The section states that parameterized queries and prepared statements separate SQL code structure from user-supplied values at the database driver level, making SQL injection impossible.

checkpoints.question: What information should users see when an application error occurs?

options.A: A generic error page with no stack traces, file paths, hostnames, or version numbers
options.B: A detailed stack trace showing the exact line of code that failed
options.C: The server hostname and version number so users know which system processed the request
options.D: SQL syntax errors so users understand what went wrong in the database query

checkpoints.explanation: The section states users should see only a generic error page with no stack traces, SQL syntax, file paths, server hostnames, or version numbers, while detailed error info goes to protected log files.

checkpoints.question: What is the primary limitation of SAST — Static Application Security Testing?

options.A: SAST requires a running application and cannot work with source code alone
options.B: SAST cannot detect runtime vulnerabilities because it analyzes code without executing it
options.C: SAST cannot find hard-coded credentials or dangerous functions in the code
options.D: SAST is too slow to integrate into CI/CD pipelines for every code commit

checkpoints.explanation: The section explicitly states that SAST cannot detect vulnerabilities that only appear at runtime, such as authentication logic flaws and business logic issues, because it never runs the code.

checkpoints.question: What can DAST — Dynamic Application Security Testing — detect that SAST cannot?

options.A: DAST can detect all code-level flaws without needing access to the application
options.B: DAST can identify hard-coded credentials and insecure randomness in source code
options.C: DAST can find authentication and session management flaws by testing a running application
options.D: DAST can discover SQL injection vulnerabilities from string concatenation patterns

checkpoints.explanation: The section states DAST finds authentication weaknesses, session management flaws, and runtime vulnerabilities that depend on application state — things SAST cannot see because SAST never executes the code.

checkpoints.question: Why does IAST — Interactive Application Security Testing — have a lower false positive rate than SAST or DAST alone?

options.A: IAST injects sensors into runtime to confirm whether a flaw is actually reachable
options.B: IAST only reports vulnerabilities found in open-source dependencies
options.C: IAST requires manual code review, which is more accurate than automated scanning
options.D: IAST accesses source code and running applications to eliminate false positives

checkpoints.explanation: The section states that IAST has a lower false positive rate than SAST or DAST alone because it can confirm whether a flaw is actually reachable during real execution.

checkpoints.question: What does Software Composition Analysis scan for?

options.A: SCA generates detailed error messages and stack traces to help debug code
options.B: SCA scans third-party dependencies for known vulnerabilities by comparing library versions
options.C: SCA monitors running applications to detect runtime authentication flaws
options.D: SCA scans source code to find SQL injection and cross-site scripting vulnerabilities

checkpoints.explanation: The section defines SCA as scanning an application's third-party dependencies for known vulnerabilities and matching library versions against vulnerability databases such as the NVD.

checkpoints.question: What type of vulnerabilities can fuzzing discover?

options.A: Fuzzing can identify logic errors in business code by analyzing source code patterns
options.B: Fuzzing can find vulnerable dependencies by scanning version numbers
options.C: Fuzzing can discover crashes, hangs, and unexpected behavior including memory corruption
options.D: Fuzzing can detect authentication weaknesses by sending malicious HTTP requests

checkpoints.explanation: The section states fuzzing automatically sends randomly generated inputs to discover crashes, hangs, and unexpected behavior, particularly memory corruption and format string vulnerabilities.

checkpoints.question: Why is it dangerous to embed secrets like credentials and API keys in source code?

options.A: Embedded secrets are visible only to developers and not to the security team
options.B: Embedded secrets prevent the use of parameterized queries in database connections
options.C: Secrets in code cause the application to run slower because they must be decrypted
options.D: Secrets in code get committed to version control and persist in history even after deletion

checkpoints.explanation: The section states that secrets embedded in code get committed to version control and persist in history even after deletion — anyone with repo access can recover them.

checkpoints.question: What does the HSTS header instruct browsers to do?

options.A: HSTS defines which sources of scripts and styles are trusted to prevent cross-site scripting
options.B: HSTS compresses HTTP responses to reduce bandwidth usage between browser and server
options.C: HSTS encrypts all cookies so they cannot be read by malicious scripts on the page
options.D: HSTS tells browsers to use only HTTPS and prevents downgrade attacks to unencrypted HTTP

checkpoints.explanation: The section defines HSTS as telling browsers to use only HTTPS and preventing downgrade attacks to unencrypted HTTP.

checkpoints.question: What is the purpose of the Content Security Policy header?

options.A: CSP forces all connections to use HTTPS instead of unencrypted HTTP
options.B: CSP defines which sources of scripts, styles, and media are trusted to limit XSS
options.C: CSP validates all user input on the server side before processing requests
options.D: CSP encrypts sensitive data in HTTP responses before sending to the browser

checkpoints.explanation: The section states that CSP defines which sources of scripts, styles, and media are trusted to limit the impact of cross-site scripting attacks.
